events.title: WHO describes COVID-19 as a pandemic
events.description: The coronavirus outbreak has spread widely across countries.

events.title: WHO lists a COVID-19 vaccine for emergency use
events.description: Its first such listing supports wider access to the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine.

events.title: Tesla reports nearly half a million deliveries
events.description: The company says it delivered about 500,000 vehicles in 2020. Deliveries measure activity, not profit.

events.title: The Fed starts raising interest rates
events.description: It raises its target for short-term rates as inflation remains high.

events.title: Webb reveals new views of space
events.description: NASA releases a full set of images from the powerful space telescope.

what_happened_next.text:
Tesla grew to more than nine times its starting value. Boeing lost about 44%, and Disney about 17%; bonds ended slightly lower. The U.S. share basket roughly doubled. The same five years could produce a huge gain or a lasting loss, depending on what a person owned.

Tesla delivered 1.79 million vehicles in 2024, far more than its 2020 total, though deliveries were slightly below 2023. Boeing reported a net loss of $11.9 billion for 2020 as the 737 MAX grounding and lower air travel hurt its airplane business. Disney’s combined streaming businesses later reported $321 million in quarterly operating income in fiscal 2024. These facts describe company changes, but do not by themselves explain the final share prices.

WHO described COVID-19 as a pandemic in March 2020 and listed its first emergency-use vaccine that December. Later, the Federal Reserve began raising interest rates in March 2022, and the Webb telescope released its first images in July. The contrast between Tesla and Boeing is enormous, but the starting page did not contain their final ranking. A broad basket reduced reliance on any one company, while its value still moved along the way.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: The new coronavirus was an international emergency. Boeing faced grounded planes, Disney celebrated a film, and Britain prepared to leave the EU.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: Single-company risks mattered. A basket spread money among many businesses, while a single share tied the result to one company’s fortunes.
reflection.what_faded_away: A box-office record or a profitable quarter did not protect a company from later shocks. Starting news described only part of the risk.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: People did not yet know how far the outbreak would spread or how economies would respond. The exact winners and losses were also unknown.

hot:2020-01:boeing.text: Boeing reported a net loss of $11.9 billion for 2020. Its commercial-airplane business faced both the long 737 MAX grounding and a sharp drop in air travel during the pandemic. These problems reduced deliveries and revenue, showing how a plane maker depends on airlines and regulators as well as its own factories.

hot:2020-01:tesla.text: Tesla delivered 1.79 million vehicles in 2024, slightly fewer than in 2023, even as it remained a much larger maker than it had been in 2020. Its fourth-quarter delivery total was 495,570. The numbers show rapid growth over time and a slower pace by the end of this window.

hot:2020-01:disney.text: Disney reported that its combined direct-to-consumer streaming businesses made $321 million in operating income in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2024. Streaming had been costly to build, so this was a sign of improving results. Parks, films and television still mattered too, and each part faced different costs.
